title: The Pulse: Global Magnetic Transit and the Infrastructure of a Connected World
body:
# The Pulse: Global Magnetic Transit and the Infrastructure of a Connected World

## What It Is

The Pulse is the circulatory system of the modern world. It is a planet-spanning network of magnetically accelerated vacuum tubes — sealed corridors bored through continental bedrock and laid across ocean floors — through which transit pods move at sustained speeds of Mach 5 to Mach 6, approximately 6,000 kilometers per hour, carrying cargo, passengers, data infrastructure, and power transmission simultaneously. The Chicago–Rotterdam corridor runs in 43 minutes. The Chicago–Lagos corridor runs in 51. The Chicago–Osaka corridor, the longest continuous Pulse route in the network at approximately 9,800 kilometers, runs in 97 minutes via a great-circle arc through the Bering Strait substrate.

The Pulse is not a recent invention. The theoretical framework for magnetic linear acceleration through evacuated tubes was established in the late twentieth century; the first commercial Pulse corridor — connecting what was then Denver to Los Angeles — opened in 2098, fourteen years before Los Angeles became uninhabitable. The technology survived the West Coast collapse. The infrastructure did not, and neither did the company that built it.

What exists now is the second generation: rebuilt from salvaged infrastructure knowledge, expanded by the corponations that understood what global connectivity was worth, and operated by a patchwork of regional authorities that are coordinated, imperfectly, by the **Pulse Interconnect Accord** — a treaty framework that is the closest thing to a functioning international agreement the post-collapse world has produced. The Accord is observed because violating it means disconnection from the network, and disconnection from the Pulse is economic death.

## The Physics

A Pulse corridor is a sealed tube, typically 4 to 6 meters in interior diameter, from which air is evacuated to approximately 0.001 atmospheres — not a true vacuum, but sufficient to reduce aerodynamic drag to negligible levels at operating speeds. The tube walls contain a series of superconducting electromagnetic coils, energized in coordinated sequence, that accelerate and decelerate pods without physical contact. There are no wheels. There is no friction surface. A pod in transit is magnetically suspended in the center of the tube at a clearance of 12 to 18 millimeters on all sides, moving through the coil sequence the way a bead moves through a series of magnets — pulled forward by the coil ahead, released by the coil behind.

Acceleration from rest to operating speed takes approximately 11 kilometers. Deceleration from operating speed to rest takes 9 kilometers. Stations — the terminal facilities where pods load and discharge — are built around these acceleration and deceleration corridors. A Pulse station is not a train platform. It is a pressurized chamber at the end of a very long gun.

The energy requirement is substantial. Operating a major Pulse corridor — the Chicago–Rotterdam Atlantic crossing, for instance — requires continuous power equivalent to a mid-sized nuclear generation facility. The Pulse is not free. The cost of a cargo slug on the Chicago–Rotterdam route is calibrated against the alternative, which is six days on a freight vessel across an increasingly storm-prone Atlantic. For most commercial purposes, the Pulse wins.

## Pods and Slugs

The vehicles that move through Pulse corridors are called **pods** in formal documentation and **slugs** in every other context. The vernacular term is accurate: a transit slug is a sealed cylinder, typically 2.4 meters in exterior diameter and between 4 and 18 meters in length, with no external features that would disrupt the magnetic suspension. It has no windows. It has no external controls. It is, from the tube's perspective, a standardized object to be accelerated.

**Cargo slugs** are the primary traffic of the Pulse network. Standardized dimensions allow automated handling at every station in the Accord network. The interior configuration is irrelevant to the tube — it can contain refrigerated biological cargo, dense metal stock, data server arrays, or processed food. Cargo slugs move continuously through the Pulse, day and night, in both directions simultaneously through parallel tube pairs. The rhythm of a Pulse station — a new slug arriving every 90 seconds on a busy corridor — is the rhythm of global trade.

**Personal slugs** are less common and more expensive. A personal slug is the same external profile as a cargo slug, but the interior is a pressurized cabin with seating for 8 to 40 passengers depending on configuration, environmental controls, and — on premium configurations — viewing screens showing externally mounted camera feeds, because the alternative is 43 minutes in a sealed cylinder with no information about the outside world, which most passengers find psychologically uncomfortable even at Mach 6.

The experience of Pulse transit is not intuitive. At operating speed, there is no sensation of motion — the tube is straight or curves so gradually that the occupant has no vestibular reference. There is no sound from outside; the vacuum eliminates it. There is a low-frequency vibration from the coil sequence, approximately 8 Hz, and a slight pressure asymmetry during acceleration and deceleration that some passengers describe as the sensation of sustained tipping. Then it stops. Then you are somewhere else. The experience is less like travel and more like being moved.

## The Network Architecture

The Pulse network is organized around **nodes** — major station facilities that serve as interchange points between multiple corridors — and **spurs**, which are single-corridor connections to secondary destinations.

**Chicago Station** is the primary node of the North American network. Since the East Coast's progressive collapse made the former primary nodes at New York, Philadelphia, and Boston nonviable, Chicago inherited the role of the continent's principal Pulse interchange. The station occupies a full city block in Zone 1, underground, operated by **Ferrogate Transit** under a Pulse Interconnect Accord franchise that is the most valuable infrastructure contract in the GLMZ. Six international corridors originate at Chicago Station. Fourteen continental spurs connect it to surviving population centers across North America. The passenger throughput is approximately 280,000 per day; cargo throughput is measured in megatonnes annually.

The Chicago–Rotterdam Atlantic corridor runs at 4,615 mph through a tube laid across the Atlantic floor at depths of 1,500 to 4,800 meters. The tube is anchored to the seafloor at intervals of 2 kilometers, with expansion joints every 400 meters to accommodate thermal variation and seafloor movement. Construction took eleven years. Forty-three construction workers died during the seafloor laying phase. There is a plaque at Chicago Station. Most passengers walk past it.

**Green Bay Node** is the primary node for the northern GLMZ and the gateway to the Canadian territories. Coldwater Logistics operates the Green Bay Node in partnership with two Canadian entities under a trilateral franchise agreement that has been renegotiated four times in twenty years and is currently six months past its renewal deadline. Traffic continues regardless.

**The Lake Crossing** — the Pulse spur from Chicago Station through Bathysphere Networks' Zone ∞ territory to the Milwaukee node — is the most-traveled internal GLMZ corridor. Ferrogate Transit operates it. Bathysphere Networks holds a perpetual easement fee that is the second-largest line item in Ferrogate's operating budget, after energy costs. Relations between the two entities are formally cordial and operationally resentful.

## Who Controls It

No single entity controls the Pulse. This is by design and by accident simultaneously.

The Pulse Interconnect Accord, drafted in 2167 by a consortium of twenty-three corponations and three surviving national governments, establishes the technical standards (pod dimensions, coil specifications, pressurization protocols), the interconnect obligations (any Accord member must accept standardized pods from any other member at Accord-compliant stations), and the dispute resolution framework (a three-judge arbitration panel that has issued 4,400 rulings in sixty years and been ignored by at least one party in approximately 400 of them).

Within the Accord framework, individual corridor segments are owned and operated by regional entities. In the GLMZ, Ferrogate Transit holds the primary franchise. In the European network, a dozen entities hold overlapping and sometimes conflicting franchises. In the Pacific network, three corponations and the remnant of the Japanese government hold joint operational authority over the same infrastructure, which produces a scheduling system that works through redundancy rather than coordination.

The effect is that the Pulse functions despite its governance rather than because of it. The technical standards are tight enough that coordination is largely automatic. The political arrangements are loose enough that no single entity can hold the network hostage. This is probably not optimal engineering. It is demonstrably stable: the Pulse has not experienced a network-wide disruption in thirty-one years, and the disruption that broke that streak lasted four hours and was caused by a maintenance contractor who misread a pressure specification.

## The Pulse and the GLMZ

The coasts failed. The Pulse connects what remains.

Chicago's position as the hub of North American Pulse infrastructure is not coincidental — it was geographic inevitability. When the East Coast nodes became nonviable and the West Coast nodes went dark, the continental Pulse network had to reorganize around whatever major nodes remained. Chicago remained. The network reorganized. The volume of traffic that once flowed through New York and Los Angeles now flows through Chicago, Milwaukee, and Green Bay, and the economic consequences of that reorientation are still working their way through the corponation structures of the GLMZ two generations later.

For Gray Zone communities, the Pulse is visible but not accessible. Chicago Station is in Zone 1 — Tier 4 sponsorship required for entry. The cost of a personal slug on any international corridor exceeds a Tier 1 resident's monthly UBC allocation by a factor of forty. The Pulse is the infrastructure of the world that the Gray Zone is adjacent to, not part of. Slugs pass overhead — or rather, below: the Pulse corridors in the GLMZ run underground, and in the Gray Zone you feel them before you see them, a faint 8 Hz vibration through the soil, the pulse of the world's circulatory system running beneath your feet.

Some Gray Zone residents who work in Zone 1 maintenance roles report that you eventually stop noticing the vibration. Others say they never do. There is a word in the Zone 3 Gray Zone vernacular — *thrumline* — for the specific sensation of standing over an active Pulse corridor, the low-frequency resonance that you feel in the bones of your feet rather than hear with your ears. It does not appear in any corponation documentation. It does not need to.
